Clouds form when atmospheric water vapor condenses into visible water droplets or ice crystals; cloud types vary by formation conditions, appearance, altitude, precipitation, and effects on weather.
Cirrus clouds form at high altitudes, about 16,500–45,000 feet, and appear as thin, wispy strands of ice crystals. They often accompany fair weather but can precede a storm.

Cumulus clouds are fluffy, cotton-like clouds that form at low to middle altitudes. They may occur in fair weather, but can develop into thunderstorm clouds when they grow tall, dark, and flat-topped.
Stratus clouds are dense, gray, low-altitude layers that can cover the sky and bring drizzle or mist.
Altostratus clouds are middle-altitude gray or blue layers that often occur before a storm; they generally produce little significant precipitation.
Cumulonimbus clouds are towering, dense clouds associated with thunderstorms. They can produce heavy rain, hail, lightning, and strong winds, and are dangerous to approach.
Stratocumulus clouds are low, puffy masses that can spread over a large area. They often appear in the morning and dissipate in the afternoon, produce little precipitation, and can block sunlight.
The user loves watching clouds and finds it fascinating that different cloud types can indicate different weather patterns.
The user described seeing a cumulonimbus cloud up close as pretty intense.
